statement: Slow tests are much more likely to be flaky: 21.0% of tests taking >10s are flaky, vs 1.5% of tests taking <0.1s (14x).

Tests that touch more of the project and more libraries are riskier: 13.7% of tests covering 101-500 source lines are flaky vs 2.1% for 26-100 lines, and 12.6% of tests using >10 third-party libraries are flaky vs 2.2% for 1-2.

Tests covering frequently changed code are riskier: with a churn score (changed_line_churn_w100) of 3-5, 21.4% of tests are flaky, vs 1.1% at 1. The very highest churn group (>5) is small (209 tests) and drops back to 2.9%, so the effect is not a straight line.

A few test smells are red flags: tests with resource optimism (23.3% flaky), fire and forget (12.1% flaky), mystery guest (12.0% flaky) are far above the 3.6% average. Smells add up: 14.3% of tests with 4+ smells are flaky vs 1.9% with exactly one. Exception: indirect testing (3.1% with vs 4.8% without) goes the other way.

Flakiness is concentrated in a few projects: alluxio (62.0%), hbase (33.6%), hector (23.2%) have the highest flaky share, and these 3 projects alone hold 36% of all flaky tests. 5 of 24 projects have at most one flaky test.
